notes: Inductive-clarity pass (2026-10-19, scratchpad brief ru-fix-brief.md): every sentence resolvable by known Russian, an adjacent contrast, a rendered SVG or a Russian gloss; one or two chapter-new lexemes per sentence (new-cluster 0); exercises reduced to three per section of 5–6 items, each using only words read by the end of its section; the three planned raster scenes stay 'planned' and carry no meaning.

Warnings left, with reasons: prior coverage 72% (floor 80%): the verb system and the naming vocabulary arrive together (23 of 35 lexemes known to the owner); answer-unknown for зову́т in the «А ты?» item and the Напиши models (the baseline chunk «Меня́ зову́т» is not chunk-matched in answers: checker limitation); stress-unverified; new-cluster.

2nd-conjugation present now productive in all persons; мочь and хоте́ть tabulated (L10). No animate masculine accusative and no object pronouns yet (Глава 6): Vera never 'sees Ivan'; she sees the children, the school, the village.
Address: Vera uses вы to Ivan (an adult) and ты to Nastya (a child); Ivan slips into ты and Marya corrects him (design §7.2, plan writer note) — paid off in Глава 32 (Order No. 1).
Glava 6 continuity: Ivan knows three letters (seen on the sign), Vera calls him Ива́н Петро́вич, the evening class is for grown men (отцы́ и сосе́ди), the slate is mended and lies on the table.

Would a peasant mother in 1913 correct her grown son's ты to the new teacher in front of her? (Plan: Marya corrects, not Vera.)

cover.alt: The new zemstvo school on its first day: a log building with two windows and a signboard over the door, village children crowding, a young woman teacher in a dark skirt and white blouse at the door, and Ivan holding his cap.
cover.art_brief: Early September 1913, a bright morning. A new log zemstvo school with a plank roof, two windows and a painted signboard over the door (the lettering is not legible in the image). Vera Nikolaevna (23, dark skirt, white high-collared blouse, hair pinned up, a shawl) stands at the door, smiling. Village children of 8–12 crowd in front, Nastya (12, kerchief, braid) at the front. Marya (50) behind them. Ivan (19, tall, fair, cap in his hands) at the back, awkward. Birch trees, autumn yellow just beginning. No legible text.

words_with_history.title: Слова́ с исто́рией
text: Фёдор кричи́т «Ва́нька»: Ва́нька — его́ брат, мла́дший.
А учи́тельница говори́т «Ива́н Петро́вич»: Ива́н — не ребёнок, и его́ оте́ц — Пётр.
И́мя — э́то кто ты. О́тчество — э́то чей ты.
words_with_history.note_en: The diminutive tells you who is speaking and how close they are: Ва́ня (warm), Ва́нька (familiar, rough), Ваню́ша (tender), Ива́н Петро́вич (respect). The proverb: 'it is never too late to learn'.

grammar.title: Говорю́, говори́шь… Вы говори́те
grammar.rule: чита́ть: чита́ю, чита́ешь, чита́ют · говори́ть: говорю́, говори́шь, говоря́т · ты ↔ вы: ты говори́шь ↔ вы говори́те
grammar.note_en: Second-conjugation verbs (говори́ть, ви́деть, люби́ть, сиде́ть…) take -ишь, -ит, -им, -ите, -ят/-ат; some change the consonant in the я form (ви́жу, сижу́, люблю́). мочь and хоте́ть are irregular. ты: family, friends, children; вы: a respected adult, or several people. A patronymic comes from the father's name, usually with -ович/-евич, -овна/-евна: Пётр → Петро́вич, Никола́й → Никола́евна. учи́тель can also be said of a woman.
